modern.description: No orthographic-tradition equivalences beyond Unicode character identity. Appropriate for contemporary printed and handwritten material; under this profile a period spelling is an out-of-lexicon word, not an allograph.

early-modern-latin-print.description: Positional letter equivalences and digraph conventions of early modern European printing: u/v and i/j positional usage (vpon, iust), w written for u (wnto), vv written for w, and the ae/oe digraph ligatures. These are facts about printing-house practice, not characters, and so must be declared rather than derived; cf. CATMuS and MUFI transcription guidance. Note the documented cost: aggressive folding can equate a rare genuine misspelling with its target (a dropped letter in a uu sequence).

early-modern-german-fraktur.description: German-language material set in Fraktur type (identified via the Churro dataset's main_script=='Latin (Fraktur variant)'). Adds the combining-e-over-vowel umlaut convention -- U+0364 COMBINING LATIN SMALL LETTER E written over a/o/u instead of a precomposed diaeresis (e.g. 'Vermoͤgen' for 'Vermögen', 'Churfuͤrſtlicher' for 'Churfürſtlicher') -- confirmed by direct inspection of Churro German-Fraktur ground truth/prediction pairs, where models silently modernize this to the precomposed form. Unlike long s (U+017F), which already has a Unicode <compat> decomposition to 's' and needs no declaration, U+0364 has no decomposition at all: Unicode does not consider 'oͤ' and 'ö' the same character, so the equivalence must be stated here or the classifier would count every recovered umlaut as a semantic error. The equivalence targets U+0364 itself (not the composed 'oͤ'/'ö' pair): fold() runs Unicode NFD/NFKD compatibility folding before applying declared equivalences, and NFD already decomposes a precomposed 'ö' into 'o' + U+0308 (combining diaeresis) -- a different combining mark from U+0364 -- so declaring 'oͤ'->'ö' would never match post-fold; mapping U+0364->U+0308 directly makes both sides converge regardless of which vowel or case it appears on. Also carries the shared pan-European early-modern print conventions (u/v, i/j) evidenced in the same rows ('vnd', 'vff').
